newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia sees attempt to disrupt presidental poll.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia sees attempt to disrupt presidental poll.

text.p: Indonesian armed forces chief General Fiesal Tanjung has warned the army to be ready for attempts to disturb a key parliamentary session next year which will select the president, the Jakarta Post reported on Saturday.
Tanjung said the military had identified parties who had attempted to foil the electoral process and the May 29 poll for the 500-member House of Representatives (DPR).
The election campaign was the most violent in the country's history.

The People's Consultative Assembly (MPR), made up of the newly elected DPR members and 500 government appointees, will meet in Jakarta in March to approve the guidelines for state policy and elect the president and vice-president.
Seventy-six year-old President Suharto, who has filled the post for almost 30 years, is widely expected to be elected unopposed for another five-year term.
"Beware of a campaign to disrupt next year's general assembly of the MPR," Tanjung said during an army cermony.

The military has blamed the unrecognised People's Democratic Party (PRD) and other unnamed "third parties" for sparking the widespread rioting, mostly on the main island of Java, that marred the 27-day official election campaign.
Authorities say more than 300 people died during the campaign, mostly from traffic accidents, while 124 died in a shopping centre fire during a riot in South Kalimantan province.
"There is a possibility that they will repeat their unconstitutional actions before the MPR's general assembly next year," Tanjung said.

Analysts have blamed widespread frustration with economic disparties as well as a backlash against the vigorous campaigning of the ruling Golkar party which angered supporters of the Moslem-oreinted United Development Party (PPP).
Both minor parties accused the government of numbers irregularities in the polls.
The PPP won just under 23 percent of the vote in the poll, which the ruling Golkar swept with a record majority of over 74 percent.
The only other party permitted to contest the election, the fragmented Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), won only three percent of the May 29 vote, down from 15 percent in 1992.
